title: Microsoft Entra ID MCP: How to Secure MCP Servers
summary: Microsoft Entra ID MCP broke at 09:12 due to an over-permissioned query. You'll find the root cause and the exact steps to apply the fix.
body_markdown:
## The over-permissioned Entra MCP query


### What Entra ID MCP is


Microsoft Entra ID MCP is Microsoft's MCP server that lets an AI assistant read your Entra identity data through Microsoft Graph, much as teams using[Activepieces](https://www.activepieces.com/) connect assistants to other systems they already run. It gives the assistant a live, permissioned path into your tenant.


What goes wrong is rarely the protocol. Someone gave that path more reach than anyone chose, and too little logging to see it. The facts here come from Microsoft's own pages, checked 16 November 2026.


### What an MCP server is


An MCP server's a small program that lets an AI assistant call another system's functions, using only the permissions you hand it. Think of a hotel key card. The card doesn't decide which rooms it opens. Whoever programmed it did.


Two terms need pinning down. Entra's Microsoft's identity service, the record of who your people are and what they may touch.


Microsoft Graph's Microsoft's single interface for reading that record and the rest of its cloud. Connect the two through MCP and the assistant can ask your directory questions in plain English.


If the permissions are too wide, the assistant can read too much, and nobody notices until the answer turns up somewhere it shouldn't.


[Activepieces](https://www.activepieces.com/) hands an assistant its 750 integrations as tools, so the same question of how much reach it gets applies well beyond Microsoft.


### An example Entra MCP privileged roles query


Here's an illustrative case, not a reported incident. At 09:12 an admin asks their assistant, "Who holds privileged roles?"


The assistant has broad directory read access, so it answers in full. Because the admin is working in a shared team chat, the full answer lands there.


Left to right, the path below runs like this. The admin's assistant sends a request through the MCP server to the directory, and the reply, a list of every privileged-role user, arrives in a chat with colleagues' avatars beside it.


Take away that the directory did nothing wrong. It answered a permitted question, and the leak happened where the answer landed.


Once it lands in that chat, the list is a map of the accounts an attacker would most like to impersonate. It sits in a place with a much wider audience than the admin ever intended.


Unless you switched logging on, nobody can say who asked or what came back.
